title: Trade Places Two by Two
statement:
You get the head of a singly linked list. Walk it in pairs: the 1st and 2nd nodes swap places, then the 3rd and 4th, and so on. If the list has an odd length, the last node stays where it is. Return the head of the new list.

Swap the nodes themselves by changing next pointers. Copying values between nodes is not allowed (the tests cannot see the difference, but an interviewer will).

Lists are written as arrays: [4, 9] is 4 → 9. An empty list is [].

examples.why: Pairs (4, 9) and (2, 7) each swap. The head changes from 4 to 9.
The 2 has no partner, so it stays last.

hints: To swap nodes A and B in the middle of a list, three pointers change. Which node, outside the pair, also has to be updated?
The node before the pair must point to B after the swap. The very first pair has no node before it; a dummy node fixes that.
Keep prev on the node before the current pair. Rewire prev → B → A → (rest), then move prev to A, which is now the second of the pair.

explain.intuition:
Swapping two neighbours A → B means three pointer changes: the node before A must now point to B, B must point to A, and A must point to whatever came after B. The easy one to forget is the first: whoever pointed at A has to be told about the swap. For the first pair that "whoever" is the caller holding head.

A dummy node in front of the head turns that special case into an ordinary one. Then you march a prev pointer forward two nodes at a time, and each step does the same three-pointer rewire. It is like reordering items in a DOM list by moving nodes, not by rewriting their text.
steps: Create dummy with dummy.next = head and set prev = dummy.
While prev.next and prev.next.next both exist, let a = prev.next and b = a.next.
Move prev = a: after the swap, a is the last node of the pair.
pitfalls: Forgetting prev.next = b: the previous pair still points to a, and b is lost from the chain.
Doing the rewires in the wrong order and losing the rest of the list. Save or set a.next = b.next before b.next is overwritten.
Returning head. After the first swap, the old head is the second node.

solutions.title: Recursion
solutions.idea: Swap the first two nodes, and let the recursive call handle everything from the third node on.

solutions.title: Iterative with a dummy node
solutions.idea: A dummy before the head gives every pair a 'previous' node, so one loop handles all pairs the same way.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def swapPairs(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        prev = dummy
        while prev.next and prev.next.next:
            a = prev.next
            b = a.next
            a.next = b.next
            b.next = a
            prev.next = b
            prev = a
        return dummy.next

followups: Reverse the nodes in groups of k instead of 2, leaving a short last group alone.
Why does the recursive version use O(n) extra memory, and when would that matter?
